6th Grade PE · Unit 1.1 · Intro to Physical Education (P.E.)
Week 1

Welcome, Sport Scientist in Training

For most of your life, movement has been instinct: you ran because you wanted to run. In 6th grade we shift the lens. This year you become a sport scientist — someone who measures, predicts, and analyzes the body. You will collect data on your own performance, test hypotheses about training, and use evidence to design plans that make you faster, stronger, and more durable.

1
Lesson 1
Why We Measure Movement

Physical activity is any movement that uses your muscles and burns energy, but for a sport scientist the more useful question is how much, how hard, and how often. Health researchers agree that kids your age should accumulate at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity per day. That number is not a guess — it comes from decades of studies linking daily movement to stronger hearts, better mood, and sharper focus.

Why does this matter at 12? Because middle school sits inside a major growth window. Bone density, heart size, and the neural wiring between brain and muscle are all being built right now. Your body treats movement as a signal: enough signal, and the hardware develops well; not enough, and the system underbuilds. The training you do this year literally shapes the body you'll carry into high school.

2
Lesson 2
Inside the Body When You Move

Open the hood on a working athlete and you see five systems running at once. Each one has a job, and a sport scientist learns to think about training as tuning each system on purpose.

❤️
Cardiovascular
Heart, blood, and vessels delivering oxygen and nutrients to working muscles and clearing waste.
🫁
Respiratory
Lungs trading oxygen in and carbon dioxide out. Faster breathing means more available fuel.
💪
Muscular
More than 600 muscles producing the forces that move bones through joints.
🦴
Skeletal
206 bones forming the frame that muscles pull against — the structural lever system of the body.
🧠
Nervous
Brain and nerves sending electrical signals to coordinate every movement, from a blink to a sprint.
🧪Sport Science

Your heart beats roughly 100,000 times each day, moving about 2,000 gallons of blood through a closed loop of vessels. During hard exercise, that rate can climb from a resting baseline of 60–90 beats per minute to over 180. The blood it pumps carries oxygen to your muscles, where it becomes the chemical fuel that powers movement. The efficiency of that whole delivery system is called your VO₂ max, and it is one of the most important numbers in sport science.

3
Lesson 3
How Movement Reshapes the Brain

Exercise is not just a body event. When you move, the brain releases chemicals called endorphins that elevate mood and reduce the perception of pain. Activity also boosts BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) — a protein that helps brain cells grow and form new connections. In short: movement is one of the strongest known signals for brain development at your age.

Kids who are active most days of the week tend to focus better in class, retain more of what they read, fall asleep faster, and recover from stress more quickly. None of that is opinion — it shows up in studies that track thousands of students over many years.

💡Did You Know?

Researchers have run brain scans on students immediately after exercise and found increased activity in the prefrontal cortex — the region you use for attention, planning, and decision-making. This is one reason a five-minute movement break can pull you out of a math slump. The effect is measurable for up to two hours after exercise.

4
Lesson 4
The Skills That Don't Show on a Stopwatch

PE also trains a different category of skill — sometimes called character skills or non-cognitive skills. These include communication, leadership, sportsmanship, and resilience. They cannot be measured with a stopwatch, but they predict success in sport, school, and work just as strongly as physical performance does.

Every game you join is a rep on these skills: cooperating with teammates, accepting an honest call against you, calling for the ball, refusing to quit after a setback. Sport scientists who study elite athletes consistently find that the mental game separates the good from the great.

🌎Real-World Connection

Top performers across sports — Simone Biles, LeBron James, Lionel Messi — credit their mental training as much as their physical training. Professional teams now employ performance psychologists who work alongside strength coaches and nutritionists. The reps you put in during a 6th-grade game build the same neural pathways an elite athlete uses to handle a championship moment.

🔬Coach's Lab

Baseline test — your resting heart rate. Sit quietly for two minutes. Then place two fingers on the side of your neck or the inside of your wrist. Count beats for 30 seconds and multiply by 2. Record that number. We'll come back to it throughout the year and watch it change as you train. Lower resting heart rate over time is one of the clearest signs your cardiovascular system is getting stronger.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Physical activity — Any movement that uses muscles and burns energy.
  • Cardiovascular system — Heart, blood, and vessels — the body's oxygen delivery network.
  • Resting heart rate — How many times your heart beats per minute at rest. Lower usually means a fitter heart.
  • Endorphins — Brain chemicals released during exercise that improve mood and dull pain.
  • BDNF — Brain-derived neurotrophic factor — a protein released by exercise that helps brain cells grow (stretch term).
  • VO₂ max — Maximum amount of oxygen your body can use during all-out exercise (stretch term).
  • Baseline — A starting measurement used to compare future results (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Data prompt: Record your resting heart rate three mornings in a row before getting out of bed. Write down all three numbers and the range (highest minus lowest). What might explain the variation between mornings — sleep, hydration, stress, what you ate the night before? Use specific evidence from your day-before to support your guess.

→What's Next

Next: launch your first VR Fitness Park assignment, then kick off Flight Club with a movement challenge that tests your new baseline.

Flight Club

Flight Club Guidelines

Welcome to Flight Club — the lab where you take everything you've studied and test it on your own body. Every other week, a new movement challenge drops. You complete it, record the data, and earn Flight Club credit. Here's how the system works.

1
Mission
What Flight Club Is

Flight Club is the active research arm of Mission: Move!. Each module ends with a Flight Club challenge — a short, focused movement task connected to that module's topic. It is where lesson content becomes experimental data.

Some challenges target strength. Some target endurance. Some test coordination, energy systems, or sportsmanship under fatigue. They are engineered to take 5–15 minutes and require minimal equipment.

2
Rules
Flight Club Rules
  1. Read the full challenge first. Know what you're doing before you start.
  2. Warm up. 2–3 minutes of light cardio plus dynamic stretches.
  3. Follow the steps in order. Don't skip — order matters.
  4. Modify, don't quit. If a move is too hard, reduce reps or scale it down. If too easy, add reps or shorten rest.
  5. Cool down. 2–3 minutes of slow movement plus static stretches.
  6. Hydrate — water before, during, and after.
  7. Submit your proof. A photo, video, or written reflection — whatever the challenge asks.
3
Crew
What Is the Flight Crew Check-In?

At the end of every challenge you'll find a Flight Crew Check-In — two short reflection questions. They aren't optional. A sport scientist trains their thinking as much as their body. The Check-In asks you to notice what you did, identify which energy system or fitness component was at work, and decide what you'd change next time.

Detailed, data-rich reflections earn extra Flight Club credit.

4
Safety
Safety First, Always
  • Check your space — clear of clutter, enough room to move
  • Wear safe shoes (closed-toe with grip)
  • Stop if something hurts beyond normal training discomfort
  • Ask a trusted adult if you're unsure about a move
💡Did You Know?

Elite athletes call recovery and self-review "the secret 1%." They spend roughly 80% of training time on training, 19% on competition — and that final 1% on reviewing what worked and what didn't. It's the smallest slice, but sport scientists who study elite performance consistently identify it as one of the strongest predictors of long-term improvement. The Flight Crew Check-In is your 1%.

→What's Next

Ready? Your first Flight Club starts in Module 1.1, Week 2. Bring your A-game.

6th Grade PE · Unit 1.2 · Warm-Ups and Cool Downs
Week 3

Warm-Ups and Cool-Downs: Priming the System

A trained sport scientist treats the warm-up as the first experiment of the workout. The goal is not to "loosen up" — it is to shift the body from a resting state to a performance state by changing temperature, blood flow, and neural readiness. Cool-downs run the same experiment in reverse, bringing the body back to baseline so recovery can begin. Both are measurable, both are skippable, and both cost you when you skip them.

1
Lesson 1
What the Warm-Up Actually Does

A warm-up is a planned 5–10 minute sequence of low-intensity movement performed before training. During those minutes, your core body temperature rises by roughly 1–2°C, your heart rate climbs gradually, and your joints lubricate with a slippery fluid called synovial fluid. Warm muscles stretch farther without injury and produce force faster — measurable differences that show up in jump-height tests and sprint times.

A complete warm-up has two phases. The general warm-up is 3–5 minutes of light cardio (jogging, jumping jacks) to raise heart rate. The dynamic warm-up follows: controlled movements like arm circles, high knees, and leg swings that move each joint through its full range and signal the nervous system to fire muscles on demand.

🧪Sport Science

Dynamic stretching (moving while you stretch) and static stretching (holding a position) produce different results. Studies show that long static holds before sprinting can actually reduce peak power by up to 5%. Dynamic stretching, in contrast, increases muscle activation and improves performance. The rule sport scientists follow: dynamic before, static after.

2
Lesson 2
What the Cool-Down Actually Does

A cool-down is a 5–10 minute slow-down period after training. It lowers your heart rate gradually, prevents blood from pooling in your legs (a major cause of dizziness right after intense effort), and gives your body a controlled return to baseline. Skipping the cool-down forces your nervous system to slam the brakes — uncomfortable, and sometimes unsafe.

A complete cool-down has three components: 2–3 minutes of light movement (walking or easy jogging), 15–30 second static stretches for the muscles you worked, and 5 deep breaths to pull your nervous system out of high-arousal mode.

💡Did You Know?

For decades, coaches blamed muscle soreness on lactate — a substance produced during hard exercise. Sport scientists have since proven that wrong. Lactate is actually a fuel your body recycles within hours, not a waste product. The next-day soreness you feel (called DOMS — delayed-onset muscle soreness) comes from microscopic tears in muscle fibers as they adapt to load. A proper cool-down speeds blood flow to those fibers and reduces how stiff you feel the next morning.

3
Try It
Five Dynamic Warm-Up Moves
🔄
Arm Circles
10 forward, 10 backward — opens shoulder joints and primes the rotator cuff.
🦵
High Knees
20 seconds at controlled pace — lifts heart rate and warms hip flexors.
↔️
Leg Swings
10 per leg, forward then sideways — activates hamstrings and inner thigh muscles.
🚶
Walking Lunges
10 steps — activates quads, glutes, and core stabilizers in one move.
🏃
Light Jog in Place
60 seconds — finishes raising core temperature and heart rate.
4
Try It
Five Cool-Down Stretches
🤲
Standing Toe Touch
Hold 20 seconds — targets hamstrings and lower back.
🦩
Quad Stretch
Pull one heel toward your glute, hold 15 seconds per side — quadriceps.
🦋
Butterfly Stretch
Sit with soles together, gently press knees down — hip adductors. Hold 30s.
💪
Shoulder Stretch
Pull one arm across your chest, 15 seconds per side — deltoid and upper back.
🌬️
Deep Breathing
5 slow breaths in through nose, out through mouth — shifts nervous system to recovery.
🌎Real-World Connection

Every professional sports team employs athletic trainers whose entire job is engineering warm-up and recovery protocols. A pro soccer team's pre-match warm-up can last 30 minutes and includes position-specific drills. NBA teams use heart-rate monitors during warm-ups to confirm each player has hit their target zone before tip-off. Pros take this seriously because the data shows it works.

🔬Coach's Lab

Test the warm-up hypothesis on your own body. Pick a measurable activity — vertical jump (mark a wall with chalk), broad jump (measure the distance), or how many push-ups you can do. Do it cold, with no warm-up, and record your result. Rest 5 minutes. Now do a full 5-minute dynamic warm-up and repeat the test. Compare numbers. Did warming up improve your performance? By how much? This is exactly how exercise scientists prove the warm-up works.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Warm-up — A planned 5–10 minute sequence of low-intensity movement done before training.
  • Cool-down — A 5–10 minute slow-down period after training to return to baseline.
  • Dynamic stretching — Controlled stretches done while moving — best before activity.
  • Static stretching — Holding a stretch position — best after activity or for flexibility training.
  • Range of motion — How far a joint can move comfortably under control.
  • DOMS — Delayed-onset muscle soreness — the next-day stiffness from training (stretch term).
  • Synovial fluid — Slippery fluid that lubricates joints; warm-ups stimulate its release (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Design a 7-minute pre-game warm-up for a sport you actually play. List exactly what you'll do, in what order, with timing. For each piece, explain whether it raises core temperature, mobilizes a specific joint, or activates a specific muscle group — and why your sport needs that particular preparation.

→What's Next

Next: build your own warm-up and cool-down routine in this week's VR assignment, then test it in Flight Club.

6th Grade PE · Unit 1.3 · Muscular Strength and Endurance
Week 5

Muscular Strength and Endurance: Building the Engine

Strength and endurance sound related, but a sport scientist treats them as two different abilities trained two different ways. Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle can produce in one effort. Muscular endurance is how long that muscle can keep producing force before it fatigues. Every athlete needs both, and the recipe for building each is different. This week we'll cover the recipe — and introduce the most important rule in all of strength training: the principle of progressive overload.

1
Lesson 1
Strength vs. Endurance

Picture your bicep as a battery. Strength is the maximum power that battery can release in one second. Endurance is how long the battery lasts before it drains. They are related, but they are not the same number.

A weightlifter trains pure strength: low reps, very heavy load. A long-distance runner trains pure endurance: very high reps of leg contractions, low load per step. Most sports sit somewhere between — a soccer player needs the endurance to run for 90 minutes and the strength to win a tackle. Knowing which one your sport demands is half the battle.

2
Lesson 2
Major Muscle Groups

The body has hundreds of muscles, but PE training focuses on the major groups — the ones that move you through space. Knowing which muscle does what makes you better at designing your own workouts.

🦵
Quadriceps
Front of the thigh. Extend the knee. Power for jumping and sprinting.
🦵
Hamstrings
Back of the thigh. Flex the knee and extend the hip. Critical for deceleration.
🍑
Glutes
The largest muscle group in the body. Powers running, jumping, and climbing.
🎯
Core
Abdominals, obliques, and lower back. Stabilizes the spine during every other movement.
💪
Biceps & Triceps
Flex and extend the elbow. Used in pulling and pushing actions.
🪶
Latissimus Dorsi
"Lats" — wide back muscles that power pull-ups, climbing, and swim strokes.
🧪Sport Science

When you train a muscle, you create microscopic tears in its fibers. During recovery — mostly while you sleep — your body repairs those tears and adds extra protein, making the muscle slightly larger and stronger. This process is called muscle protein synthesis, and it peaks within the first 24–48 hours after a workout. There's an important practical consequence: rest days are not optional. They are when the actual building happens.

3
Lesson 3
The FITT Principle and Progressive Overload

Sport scientists organize every training plan around a four-letter framework called FITT:

  • Frequency — how often you train (sessions per week)
  • Intensity — how hard each session is (weight, speed, effort)
  • Time — how long each session lasts (minutes, sets, reps)
  • Type — what kind of exercise (cardio, strength, flexibility, sport-specific)

Change any of these four variables and you change the training stress. The most powerful idea in strength training is progressive overload: to keep getting stronger, you have to gradually increase the demand. Same workout every week = your body adapts, then plateaus. Slowly add reps, sets, or resistance, and the body keeps adapting upward.

💡Did You Know?

The strongest muscle in your body — relative to its size — is the masseter, the muscle that closes your jaw. It can produce up to 200 pounds of force on your back teeth. But the largest and most powerful muscle group overall is the gluteus maximus. Sport scientists studying sprinters have found that the size of an athlete's glutes is one of the best predictors of acceleration speed in the first 10 meters of a sprint.

4
Try It
Bodyweight Strength Circuit

You don't need weights to train strength — your own body is a complete resistance system. Try this circuit, then come back next week and try to add 1–2 reps. That's progressive overload in action.

🦾
Push-Ups
10 reps. Trains chest, shoulders, triceps, and core.
🏋️
Squats
15 reps. Trains quads, glutes, and hamstrings as one chain.
📏
Plank Hold
30 seconds. Tests core endurance in isometric load.
🌉
Glute Bridges
12 reps. Targets the glutes and lower back.
🌎Real-World Connection

Strength training extends far past sports. Firefighters need it to carry equipment up stairs. Nurses need it to lift patients safely. Construction workers need it to swing tools all day. Even office workers train strength to protect their backs from a lifetime of sitting. The strength foundation you build at 12 is part of a body you'll carry for the next 80+ years.

🔬Coach's Lab

Map your one-week progress curve. Do as many push-ups as you can with good form. Record the number. Train push-ups every other day this week (10–15 reps, 3 sets). On Day 7, re-test your max. Did your number go up? By how many? If it didn't move, examine your variables: did you actually train 3 sessions, or skip one? Did you sleep enough? This is how a coach diagnoses a plateau — by looking at the data, not guessing.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Muscular strength — Maximum force a muscle can produce in a single effort.
  • Muscular endurance — How long a muscle can produce force before fatiguing.
  • Rep / repetition — One complete cycle of an exercise.
  • Set — A group of reps performed without rest.
  • FITT principle — Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type — the four variables of any training plan (stretch term).
  • Progressive overload — Gradually increasing training demand over time to keep adapting (stretch term).
  • Muscle protein synthesis — The repair-and-rebuild process that makes muscles stronger after training (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Using the FITT principle, design a 2-week strength program for a sport you play. Specify Frequency (how many days), Intensity (how heavy or how hard), Time (sets and reps), and Type (which exercises). Justify each choice — why this F, this I, this T, this T for your sport? Then describe how you would apply progressive overload from Week 1 to Week 2.

→What's Next

Next: build your own strength workout in the Strength Building Activities assignment, then test your endurance in Flight Club.

pages.html:

6th Grade PE · Unit 1.4 · Cardiovascular Fitness
Week 7

Cardiovascular Fitness: Training the Engine

Cardiovascular fitness is how well your heart, lungs, and blood vessels work together to deliver oxygen to working muscles. It is the single most powerful predictor of long-term health that scientists have ever measured. This week we'll look inside the system, then meet two of the three energy pathways your body uses — and learn the heart-rate zones every sport scientist uses to design cardio training.

1
Lesson 1
The System, Inside Out

The cardiovascular system is a closed loop with three main parts. The heart is a fist-sized muscle that pumps roughly 100,000 times a day. Blood vessels — arteries, veins, and tiny capillaries — form the highway. Blood itself carries oxygen and nutrients out to muscles and waste products like carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

The loop works like this: you breathe in, your lungs pull oxygen out of the air, your heart pumps that oxygen-loaded blood to working muscles, the muscles use the oxygen to produce energy, and the now low-oxygen blood returns to the lungs to reload. Train the system and every step gets more efficient.

🧪Sport Science

Elite athletes have a measurable number called VO₂ max — the maximum volume of oxygen the body can use during all-out exercise. Untrained adults usually score around 35–40 ml/kg/min. Tour de France winners have measured above 80. The good news is VO₂ max is highly trainable, especially in adolescence — kids who start cardio training young raise their lifelong ceiling.

2
Lesson 2
Energy Systems: ATP-PC, Glycolytic, Oxidative

Your muscles run on a chemical called ATP (adenosine triphosphate). But your body has three different ways to produce it, and each one dominates at a different effort level:

⚡
ATP-PC System
All-out efforts under 10 seconds. Used for sprints, jumps, and explosive lifts. No oxygen needed.
🔥
Glycolytic System
Hard efforts from 10 seconds to about 2 minutes. Burns carbs without oxygen. Used in 400m sprints.
🫁
Oxidative System
Anything past 2 minutes. Uses oxygen to burn carbs and fat. Powers distance running and cycling.

Sport scientists call the first two anaerobic ("without oxygen") and the third aerobic ("with oxygen"). A basketball player taps all three in a single possession: aerobic jogging up the court, glycolytic during a 30-second press, ATP-PC for the jump shot.

3
Lesson 3
Heart Rate and the Five Training Zones

You can estimate your maximum heart rate with a rough formula: 220 minus your age. For a 12-year-old, that's about 208 beats per minute. Sport scientists divide everything below that maximum into five heart rate zones — each one trains a different system.

  • Zone 1 (50–60% of max) — Very easy. Recovery, warm-up.
  • Zone 2 (60–70%) — Conversational pace. Builds aerobic base.
  • Zone 3 (70–80%) — Comfortably hard. Improves endurance.
  • Zone 4 (80–90%) — Hard. Pushes lactate threshold.
  • Zone 5 (90–100%) — All-out. Trains VO₂ max and ATP-PC.

Most of your weekly cardio should sit in Zones 2 and 3. Short bursts in Zone 5 are powerful but you can't sustain them — they should be used sparingly, with full recovery between.

💡Did You Know?

Trained endurance athletes can have resting heart rates as low as 40 BPM — about half the rate of an average adult. The reason is not that their heart is weak. It's the opposite: each beat moves so much blood that the heart can fire less often. This number (stroke volume) is one of the clearest signs of cardiovascular adaptation.

4
Try It
Cardio Training Options
🏃
Steady Jog
10–20 minutes in Zone 2. Foundation of aerobic fitness.
🚴
Bike Ride
Low-impact aerobic option. Easy to control intensity.
⚡
Sprint Intervals
8 rounds of 20s all-out / 40s walk. Trains ATP-PC and glycolytic.
🏊
Swimming
Full-body aerobic work with almost no joint impact.
🪜
Stair Climbing
Combines leg power with cardiac demand. Highly efficient.
💃
Dance
Continuous high-energy dance routines deliver real Zone 3 cardio.
🌎Real-World Connection

Cardiovascular fitness is one of the strongest predictors of lifespan that scientists have ever measured. Adults in the top 20% for cardio fitness live an average of 5–7 years longer than those in the bottom 20%, even after controlling for diet and weight. The cardiovascular habits you build at 12 set up the heart you'll have at 70.

🔬Coach's Lab

Calculate your heart-rate recovery rate. Do 60 seconds of vigorous jumping jacks. Immediately take your pulse (count for 15 seconds, multiply by 4). Wait exactly one minute, then take it again. Subtract: the difference is your 1-minute heart rate recovery. A drop of more than 25 BPM is good. A drop under 12 means your cardiovascular system has room to grow. Re-test in 4 weeks of training and compare.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Cardiovascular fitness — How well the heart, lungs, and vessels deliver oxygen during exercise.
  • Aerobic — Activity that uses oxygen as the main energy source. Sustained, moderate effort.
  • Anaerobic — Short, intense activity that does not rely on oxygen. Sprints and explosive moves.
  • Heart rate zone — A percentage range of your max heart rate, used to target specific training adaptations.
  • ATP-PC system — The energy pathway for efforts under 10 seconds — sprints, jumps (stretch term).
  • Glycolytic system — Energy pathway for efforts of 10s–2 min, no oxygen needed (stretch term).
  • Oxidative system — Aerobic energy pathway used for any effort past 2 minutes (stretch term).
  • VO₂ max — Maximum rate the body can use oxygen during exercise (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Data prompt: Time yourself running the same loop or distance on Monday and again on Friday after three days of Zone 2 jogging. Record both times and your heart rate immediately after each run. Did the time improve? Did the post-run heart rate drop? If both improved, you have evidence of a training effect. If only one improved, what does that tell you about which system is adapting first?

→What's Next

Next: design your own cardio plan in this week's My Cardio Plan assignment, then push your heart rate up in Flight Club.

pages.html:
Optima

Mission: Move!
6th Grade PE · Unit 1.5 · Flexibility and Stretching
Week 9

Flexibility and Stretching: Training Your Range

Flexibility is the ability of your muscles and joints to move through their full range of motion. It sounds quieter than strength or speed, but every other physical skill is built on top of it. A pitcher with a stiff shoulder cannot throw fast. A runner with tight hips cannot extend at full stride. A goalkeeper who cannot drop into a split gives up the corner. This week we look at why flexibility matters, the science of how stretching works, and how to design a routine that actually changes your body.

1
Lesson 1
What Flexibility Really Is

Bones move because muscles pull on them. Each muscle crosses one or more joints, and the muscle's length determines how far the joint can travel. When the muscle is short and tight, the joint moves only a little. When the muscle is long and supple, the joint moves through a full arc.

Flexibility is not one number — it is joint-specific. You might have flexible shoulders and tight hips, or supple hamstrings and a stiff back. A good sport scientist tests each major joint separately, then designs training to fix the limiters that are holding back actual sport performance.

2
Lesson 2
Active vs. Passive Flexibility

Two kinds of flexibility behave differently in sport:

  • Active flexibility — how far you can move a joint using only your own muscles. Example: lifting your leg as high as you can without grabbing it.
  • Passive flexibility — how far the joint moves with outside help (a partner, gravity, your hands pulling). Example: lying on your back and pulling your knee toward your chest.

Passive range is almost always greater than active range, but in a game you only get to use the active version. That gap — the difference between what you could stretch to and what you can actively reach — is where injuries often happen.

🧪Sport Science

Inside every muscle are tiny sensors called muscle spindles. When a muscle stretches quickly, these sensors fire a protective reflex that tells the muscle to contract — preventing damage. This is why fast, bouncy stretches don't work well. A slow stretch held for 15–30 seconds lets the spindles relax, and the muscle actually lengthens. Hold that stretch consistently over weeks, and the muscle's resting length increases — a real, measurable change.

3
Lesson 3
Dynamic vs. Static Stretching

Flexibility training uses two methods at different times:

  • Dynamic stretching — moving stretches done before activity. Improves performance and warms tissue.
  • Static stretching — holding a position after activity or in a stand-alone session. The method for building long-term flexibility.

Real flexibility gains require 3–5 static-stretch sessions per week for at least 4 weeks. One session changes nothing. A habit changes everything. Sport scientists call this the principle of specificity — your body adapts to the exact stress you give it, and only that stress, only if you give it enough times.

4
Try It
Five Core Static Stretches
🦋
Butterfly
Sit with soles together, gently press knees down. Targets adductors. 30s.
🦩
Quad Stretch
Stand on one leg, pull other heel to glute. 20s per side.
🤲
Toe Touch
Stand, slowly reach toward toes. Hamstrings + lower back. 30s.
🐶
Downward Dog
Hands and feet on floor, hips up. Calves, hamstrings, shoulders.
🐍
Cobra
Lie face down, press chest up with arms. Opens front of body.
💡Did You Know?

Gymnasts and ballet dancers don't have naturally elastic bodies — most start training before age 6 and stretch for 1–2 hours every single day for years. That's the dose required to reach a full split or a backbend. The takeaway is honest: flexibility is earned through consistent reps, not gifted at birth. Even 10 minutes a day, done 4 days a week, produces measurable change in 4 weeks.

🔬Coach's Lab

Test active vs. passive flexibility on your own hip. Lie on your back. Lift one leg as high as you can without using your hands — that's your active range. Mark where it stops (against a wall, or count tiles on the ceiling). Then grab behind your thigh and pull as far as it'll comfortably go — that's your passive range. Subtract: the gap between the two is your strength deficit at end-range. A big gap means your muscles aren't strong enough to use the flexibility you already have. That changes the kind of training you need.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Flexibility — The ability of a muscle or joint to move through its full range.
  • Range of motion — How far a joint can move comfortably under control.
  • Active flexibility — Range you can reach using only your own muscles.
  • Passive flexibility — Range you can reach with outside help.
  • Specificity — Training principle: your body adapts only to the exact stress you give it (stretch term).
  • Muscle spindle — Sensor inside a muscle that fires a reflex to prevent overstretching (stretch term).
  • Adductor — Muscle group on the inner thigh that pulls the leg toward the body's midline (stretch term).
🌎Real-World Connection

NFL kickers spend 20+ minutes before every game opening hip flexors — if the hip can't fully extend, the kick loses power. NBA centers work for hours weekly on ankle and hip mobility so they can land safely from jumps. Sport scientists at the U.S. Olympic Training Center test flexibility on every incoming athlete because they know the limiter on performance is usually a tight joint, not a weak muscle.

📝Weekly Reflection

Data prompt: Measure how far you can reach in a seated toe-touch today. Use a yardstick or count fingertips past your toes (or how many inches short). Stretch hamstrings 3 days this week (3 holds × 30 seconds each day). Re-measure on Day 8. What changed? If your number didn't move, examine the variables: did you actually stretch the right muscle, hold long enough, do enough sessions? Use the data to diagnose.

pages.title: Week 11: Nutrition
pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
6th Grade PE · Unit 1.6 · Nutrition
Week 11

Nutrition: Fueling the Athlete

A sport scientist treats food the same way they treat training — as input that creates measurable output. The energy you eat becomes the fuel that powers your muscles, the protein that rebuilds your fibers, and the chemistry your brain uses to focus. This week we'll cover macronutrients, micronutrients, hydration, and one of the most important applied concepts in sports nutrition: the protein synthesis window.

1
Lesson 1
The Three Macronutrients

Nearly every food gives you some mix of three macronutrients — the big-volume nutrients your body needs in significant amounts. Each one has a specific job:

🍞
Carbohydrates
The body's preferred fuel for movement. Found in grains, fruits, vegetables, dairy.
🍗
Proteins
Building blocks for muscles, bones, skin, and blood. Found in meat, eggs, beans, dairy, nuts.
🥑
Fats
Long-lasting energy plus structural support for organs and brain cells. Found in oils, nuts, avocado, fish.

You need all three. Cutting out any category — all fat, all carbs — leaves a system short on something it needs. Sport scientists who study eating disorders in young athletes call this one of the most damaging patterns in youth sport.

2
Lesson 2
Micronutrients, Water, and Electrolytes

Beyond macros, the body needs much smaller doses of micronutrients — vitamins and minerals — to keep the system running:

  • Vitamin C — supports wound healing and immune function (citrus, peppers, strawberries)
  • Calcium — builds bone density during growth years (milk, yogurt, leafy greens)
  • Iron — helps blood carry oxygen (red meat, beans, spinach)
  • Potassium — keeps muscle contractions firing cleanly and prevents cramps (bananas, potatoes)

Then there's water. Your body is about 60% water by mass, and even mild dehydration (a 2% loss) measurably reduces strength, endurance, and concentration. During hard sweat you also lose electrolytes — sodium, potassium, magnesium — which is why athletes use sports drinks for long sessions and plain water for shorter ones.

When fluid loss goes too far — especially in heat — simple dehydration can climb into a heat illness. Sport scientists track three types tied to fluid and electrolyte loss, and they form a ladder you never want to climb:

  • Heat cramps — painful muscle spasms (often in the calves or stomach) from fluid and electrolyte loss. The earliest warning sign.
  • Heat exhaustion — heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, weakness, and a racing pulse. The body is losing the cooling battle: stop, get to shade, hydrate, and cool down.
  • Heat stroke — a medical emergency. The body stops cooling itself, the skin turns hot, sweating may stop, and thinking gets confused. Get help immediately.

The fix is the same at every rung: hydrate before you feel thirsty, take breaks in the heat, and cool down early. Catch the cramps and you never reach the stroke.

🧪Sport Science

When you eat carbs, the body breaks them into glucose. Glucose either gets used immediately as fuel or gets stored in muscles and liver as glycogen. During hard training, muscles tap into that glycogen reserve. Distance athletes "carb load" before big events because they want their glycogen tanks full at the start — empty tanks at mile 20 of a marathon is the famous "bonk."

3
Lesson 3
Eat the Rainbow

Different colored fruits and vegetables contain different vitamins, minerals, and plant compounds called phytonutrients. The more colors on your plate, the broader the range of nutrients you receive — and the stronger your overall health markers tend to be.

🍎
Red
Tomatoes, strawberries, peppers. Contains lycopene, good for heart health.
🥕
Orange/Yellow
Carrots, sweet potatoes, oranges. Beta-carotene supports eyes and immune system.
🥦
Green
Broccoli, spinach, kale. Folate, iron, calcium, magnesium.
🫐
Blue/Purple
Blueberries, eggplant, purple grapes. Anthocyanins for brain health.
🧄
White
Garlic, onions, cauliflower. Sulfur compounds support immune function.
💡Did You Know?

Your gut contains trillions of bacteria that help digest food and even communicate with your brain through what scientists call the gut-brain axis. This community of microbes (the "microbiome") affects mood, immune function, and energy. The single strongest way to build a healthy microbiome is to eat a wide variety of plants — the more different fruits, vegetables, beans, and whole grains you eat in a week, the more diverse and resilient your gut community becomes.

4
Lesson 4
Building a Plate and Timing Protein

The simplest applied tool for daily eating is the MyPlate model from the USDA:

  • ½ of your plate — fruits and vegetables
  • ¼ of your plate — grains (preferably whole grains)
  • ¼ of your plate — protein
  • A side — dairy or a calcium alternative

For athletes, there's a useful nuance called the protein synthesis window. The 1–2 hours right after training is when your body is most primed to rebuild muscle from food. Getting 15–25 grams of protein in that window — a glass of milk, a yogurt, a piece of chicken — measurably boosts recovery and gain.

🌎Real-World Connection

Pro athletes work with sports dietitians who plan meals down to the gram. An NBA player might consume 4,000 calories a day during the season, carefully timed around practices. An Olympic gymnast might eat closer to 2,000 with extra protein and calcium for bone health. Different sport demands = different fuel plans. The principle stays the same: match the input to the system you're training.

5
Lesson 5
Fact vs. Fallacy: Be a Smart Fitness Consumer

The fitness industry sells billions of dollars of products every year — supplements, "fat-burning" teas, miracle machines, and training programs. A sport scientist treats every claim the way they treat a hypothesis: show me the evidence. Learning to tell a fact (supported by repeated, controlled studies) from a fallacy (a claim that only sounds scientific) protects both your money and your health.

Run these four tests on any fitness or nutrition claim you see:

  • Too good to be true? "Lose 10 pounds in a week without exercise" ignores how the body actually works. Real change is gradual.
  • Who profits? If the company making the claim also sells the product, be skeptical — look for independent evidence.
  • Where's the study? "Studies show" means nothing without a real, repeatable study. One testimonial is a story, not data.
  • Does it replace the basics? No product out-performs consistent training, real food, sleep, and hydration. Anything claiming to is selling a fallacy.
💡Did You Know?

One of the most common fitness fallacies is spot reduction — the idea that doing crunches burns belly fat specifically. Decades of controlled studies show the body pulls fat from all over, not from the muscle you happen to be working. Crunches build the abdominal muscle underneath; they don't selectively burn the fat on top of it. Any product promising to "melt fat" from one body part is selling a fallacy.

🔬Coach's Lab

Run a one-day energy-balance audit. Energy works like a bank account: calories in (food) versus calories out (activity). (1) Log everything you ate and drank yesterday and, using package labels or a free nutrition app, estimate your total calories consumed. (2) List your physical activity for the day and estimate the energy expended — most fitness trackers and apps give a rough calorie burn (a moderate hour of activity is very roughly 300–500 calories for a 12-year-old). (3) Tag each food item mostly carb, protein, fat, or mixed. Now compare: was your day closer to balance, a surplus (more in than out), or a deficit? Describe what your data shows and one thing you would adjust. This is an estimate to build awareness — not a number to obsess over.

6
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Macronutrients — The three large-volume nutrients: carbs, protein, fat.
  • Micronutrients — Vitamins and minerals — small amounts, essential function.
  • Carbohydrates — Body's preferred fuel for movement.
  • Protein — Nutrient used to build and repair tissue.
  • Glycogen — Stored form of carbohydrates in muscles and liver (stretch term).
  • Electrolytes — Minerals like sodium and potassium that conduct electrical signals in nerves and muscles (stretch term).
  • Protein synthesis window — The 1–2 hours after training when the body is most primed to rebuild muscle (stretch term).
  • Dehydration — A measurable drop in body water that hurts strength, endurance, and focus.
  • Heat illness — A ladder of conditions — heat cramps, heat exhaustion, heat stroke — caused by fluid and electrolyte loss in heat (stretch term).
  • Fact vs. fallacy — Telling an evidence-backed claim (fact) from one that only sounds scientific (fallacy).
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: Plan a one-day eating schedule for a 12-year-old athlete who has soccer practice from 5–6:30 PM. Write out breakfast, lunch, a pre-practice snack, a post-practice meal, and dinner. For each one, name the dominant macronutrient and justify why that macro fits that moment in the day (fuel, recovery, sleep prep).

→What's Next

Next: design a healthy plate in Week 12, then test your fuel choices in Flight Club.

pages.title: Week 13: Locomotor Skills
pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
6th Grade PE · Unit 1.7 · Locomotor Skills
Week 13

Locomotor Skills: The Movement Alphabet

Every athletic skill is built from locomotion — moving the body from one place to another. Sport scientists count eight foundational locomotor patterns, and they are the alphabet of athletic movement. A sprinter, a goalkeeper, a dancer, and a basketball point guard all combine these eight patterns into something more complex. Master the alphabet, and the advanced moves become readable.

1
Lesson 1
The Eight Locomotor Skills

PE teachers and biomechanists group fundamental movement into eight patterns. Each one uses the legs differently, and each one stresses a different combination of strength, balance, and timing.

🚶
Walking
One foot always on the ground. Heel strikes first, toe pushes off.
🏃
Running
Both feet leave the ground briefly between steps. Includes a true flight phase.
🦘
Hopping
Push off and land on the same foot — tests single-leg power and balance.
🤾
Jumping
Push off two feet, land on two feet. Tests bilateral power.
🐴
Galloping
One foot leads, the other catches up. Same lead foot stays in front.
⏭️
Skipping
Step + hop, alternating sides. Step-hop, step-hop.
↔️
Sliding
Sideways movement — one foot leads, the other catches up.
🦌
Leaping
Push off one foot, land on the other foot. Asymmetric power transfer.
🧪Sport Science

The brain region that controls locomotor patterns is the motor cortex — a strip across the top of the brain. Every time you practice a movement, the connection between neurons gets stronger and the signal gets faster, a process called myelination. Eventually the pattern becomes automatic — what athletes call "muscle memory." It is not stored in muscles; it is stored in the brain as a faster, smoother neural pathway.

2
Lesson 2
Why Locomotor Variety Matters

You probably perform most of these patterns without thinking. So why drill them in PE? Because real games demand fast switching between patterns under pressure. A soccer player jogs, sprints, slides to defend, then leaps over a tackle — all in five seconds. A basketball player shuffles on defense, gallops on a fast break, then jumps to rebound. Smooth transitions = faster, more efficient athletes.

Locomotor work also stresses the principle of specificity: your body adapts to the exact pattern you practice. Train only forward running and your sideways slide stays slow. Train all eight, and your overall movement vocabulary grows.

3
Lesson 3
Biomechanics: Ground Reaction Force

Here's a foundational biomechanics idea: every time your foot pushes down on the ground, the ground pushes back with equal force. Sport scientists call this ground reaction force (GRF). When you sprint, your foot strikes the ground with up to 3–5 times your body weight, and the ground returns that force into your stride.

This explains why technique matters so much. A sprinter who lands cleanly on the ball of the foot uses GRF efficiently. A runner who heel-strikes hard loses energy to the ground absorbing the impact. Same body, different mechanics, very different speed.

💡Did You Know?

Astronauts returning from the International Space Station have to re-learn walking. After six months in microgravity, their brain forgets how heavy their body is on Earth and how much ground reaction force their legs need to push against. NASA puts them through structured locomotor rehab — basically the same eight patterns you're working on — to rebuild the motor program. It's a striking reminder that "automatic" skills are actually maintained by daily use.

4
Try It
Locomotor Skill Circuit

Run this 4-minute circuit: 30 seconds on each pattern, no rest between. Focus on quality, not speed.

  1. Walk forward with deliberate heel-to-toe contact
  2. Jog at a steady, controlled pace
  3. Hop on the right foot, then switch to the left at the halfway point
  4. Jump in place with soft, controlled landings
  5. Gallop forward, then switch lead leg
  6. Skip with high knees and tall posture
  7. Slide sideways — left direction, then right
  8. Leap forward over an imaginary line, focus on soft landing
🌎Real-World Connection

Olympic-level track coaches still use locomotor drills with elite sprinters. "A-skips" and "B-skips," high-knee runs, and side shuffles appear in nearly every world-class warm-up. The basics never stop being useful — coaches just refine them to extract more force and less waste. Usain Bolt's warm-up still includes skipping.

🔬Coach's Lab

Measure your own ground reaction force indirectly. Find a wall and mark your standing reach (highest point you can touch flat-footed). Then do a max vertical jump and mark the top of your jump in chalk. Subtract: that's your vertical leap. The higher your jump, the more force your legs produced against the ground. Re-test in 2 weeks of single-leg hop drills (3×/week). Did the number improve? Specificity in action.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Locomotion — Moving the body from one place to another.
  • Locomotor skills — The 8 fundamental movement patterns: walk, run, hop, jump, gallop, skip, slide, leap.
  • Hop — Push off and land on the same foot.
  • Leap — Push off one foot, land on the other foot.
  • Motor cortex — The brain region that controls voluntary movement (stretch term).
  • Ground reaction force — The push-back the ground gives your foot when it strikes — a key biomechanics concept (stretch term).
  • Specificity — Your body adapts to the exact pattern you train, and only that pattern (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Data prompt: Pick your weakest locomotor skill from the eight above (be honest). Time yourself doing 20 reps with good form. Practice it 3 times this week (5 minutes per session). Re-time on Day 8. Did your time drop? If yes, what specifically improved — speed, balance, rhythm? If no, examine: was your practice quality or just quantity?

→What's Next

Next: log your locomotor skills in this week's project, then test your patterns in Flight Club.

pages.html:
Optima

6th Grade PE · Unit 1.8 · Throwing and Catching
Week 15

Throwing and Catching: Sending and Receiving

Throwing and catching are manipulative skills — movements where the body controls an object rather than just moving itself. They look simple, but a good throw involves a precise sequence of body segments firing in order: legs, hips, core, shoulder, elbow, wrist, fingers. Time the sequence right and the ball flies fast and straight. Time it wrong and the ball flutters.

1
Lesson 1
The Mechanics of an Overhand Throw

A powerful overhand throw uses the entire body, not just the arm. Power moves from the ground up, with each segment of the body adding speed to the next. Here is the sequence:

  1. Stand sideways — the non-throwing shoulder points at the target
  2. Step toward the target with the opposite foot (right hand throws → left foot steps)
  3. Rotate the hips as the foot lands and the body weight transfers forward
  4. Drive the throwing shoulder forward as hip rotation completes
  5. Whip the arm through — elbow leads, hand follows
  6. Snap the wrist on release for spin and accuracy
  7. Follow through — the hand finishes near the opposite hip

Each step transfers energy to the next, like cracking a whip. Skip any step — like throwing using only your arm — and most of the available power is lost.

🧪Sport Science

This sequence has a name in biomechanics: the kinetic chain. Major League Baseball pitchers generate roughly 50% of their throwing velocity from their legs and hips alone. The arm is just the final link that releases the accumulated energy. That is why elite pitchers spend a huge chunk of their offseason in the weight room building lower-body strength. Stronger legs literally throw harder fastballs.

2
Lesson 2
Catching: Tracking, Positioning, Receiving

Catching looks like one skill but is really three working together:

  • Tracking — keeping the eyes on the ball from release to arrival
  • Positioning — moving the body so the ball arrives in front of the chest
  • Receiving — using "soft hands" that give a little on impact so the ball doesn't bounce out

For most middle schoolers, positioning is the limiter. You have to move your feet, not just reach with your arms. Watch a great outfielder: they are moving the instant the bat makes contact, and by the time the ball arrives they're already underneath it. Great catchers are great foot-movers first.

3
Lesson 3
Throws for Different Situations

The right throw depends on the distance, accuracy needed, and how much time you have.

🎯
Overhand Throw
Long distance, maximum power. Baseball outfield, football, javelin.
🥎
Underhand Toss
Short distance, gentle arc. Softball pitch, beanbag toss, dodgeball roll.
🏀
Two-Handed Pass
Fast and accurate. Basketball chest pass, soccer throw-in.
⚾
Sidearm
Lower release angle, faster. Quick infield throws, skipping a stone.
💡Did You Know?

Humans are the only animals that throw with both speed and accuracy. Chimpanzees can throw, but only at about 20 mph and rarely on target. The human shoulder joint evolved a uniquely flexible structure that lets the arm whip forward at speeds no other primate can match. Anthropologists think this throwing ability gave early humans a major survival advantage — both for hunting and for defense. When you make a great throw, you're using one of the oldest distinctly human athletic skills.

4
Try It
Throw and Catch Drills
🧱
Wall Throw
Throw against a wall, catch the rebound. 20 reps each hand.
🪣
Bucket Toss
Underhand toss into a bucket from 5 feet. Move it back as accuracy improves.
👥
Partner Catch
Throw and catch with a partner from 10 feet. Step into every throw.
👆
Wall Catch
Toss the ball up, catch with both hands. Then one hand. Then with a clap between!
🌎Real-World Connection

NFL quarterbacks throw a football about 60 mph with pinpoint accuracy at moving targets while being chased by 300-pound defenders. They train this skill with thousands of reps a week. The exact same kinetic chain you are learning — sideways stance, step, hip rotation, follow-through — is what a Super Bowl winner uses. The pros have just done it tens of millions more times.

🔬Coach's Lab

Diagnose your own throwing kinetic chain. Throw a tennis ball at a wall, hard but with control. Have a partner record a slow-motion video on a phone. Watch the video and check three things: (1) Did your opposite foot step toward the target? (2) Did your hips rotate before your arm came forward? (3) Did your hand finish near your opposite hip? Score yourself 0–3. The missing piece is your first thing to fix.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
🎯 Words to Know
  • Manipulative skills — Movements that involve controlling an object — ball, racket, bat.
  • Overhand throw — The arm comes over the shoulder — used for distance and power.
  • Underhand toss — The arm swings below the shoulder — used for short, soft passes.
  • Kinetic chain — Sequence of body segments transferring force from ground to ball (stretch term).
  • Follow-through — Continuing the motion after release — adds power and accuracy.
  • Soft hands — Hands that give a little on impact so the ball doesn't bounce out.
  • Center of gravity — The balance point of the body during movement (stretch term).
📝Weekly Reflection

Design prompt: A teammate's throws are consistently weak and inaccurate. Using the seven-step kinetic chain, design a 3-drill diagnostic plan to figure out which step in their chain is broken. Describe each drill, what specifically you'd watch for, and what you'd recommend if the problem is at the hips vs. the wrist.

→What's Next

Next: sharpen your catching in Week 16's "Catch Me If You Can!" challenge, then test your hands in Flight Club.

🚀 Flight Club Challenge

Kick off your sport-scientist-in-training journey with three classic mobility moves. These open up your shoulders, back, and neck — the joints you'll mobilize in nearly every Flight Club to come.

1
Reach for the Sky Stretch

How to Do It:

  • Stand up tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
  • Stretch both arms up as high as possible, reaching for the sky.
  • Hold for 10 seconds, then relax.
  • Optional: Wiggle your fingers like you're grabbing stars!

Benefits: Stretches arms, shoulders, and back.

2
Hug Yourself Stretch

How to Do It:

  • Wrap your arms around yourself like you're giving a big hug.
  • Gently pull your shoulders forward while keeping your back straight.
  • Hold for 10 seconds, then switch arm positions (whichever arm was on top, switch it).

Benefits: Stretches shoulders and upper back.

3
Shoulder Rolls

How to Do It:

  • Stand or sit up straight.
  • Slowly roll your shoulders forward in a circular motion 5 times.
  • Then roll your shoulders backward 5 times.

Benefits: Loosens up the shoulders and neck.

🏃Activity Cue

Submit a video demonstrating the challenges. The more you do, the more points you get in Flight Club!

Flight Crew, check in!

Toe Touch Stretch (Waterfall Stretch)

Your results are private. They go only to you and your teacher, are used to set your personal training goals, and are never posted or compared publicly.

Five Events, Five Fitness Components
EventWhat it measuresHow to run it at home

  3. Slowly bend both knees to lower your body straight down.

  3. At the same time, lift your arms, chest, and legs slightly off the ground.
  4. Try to hold this pose for 10 seconds — like you're flying through the sky!
  5. Slowly lower back down and rest. Try it again 2–3 more times!

Benefits: Strengthens your back and core muscles.

3
Bench Dips
  1. Find a sturdy chair, bench, or low table. Sit on the edge with your hands next to your hips.
  2. Walk your feet forward and slide your bottom off the edge, so your hands are holding you up.
  3. Bend your elbows to lower your body a little — like you're going down slowly.
  4. Push back up until your arms are straight again.
  5. Try doing 5–10 dips, then take a break!

🚀 Flight Club Challenge

Mix of flexibility and core work. These three target the muscle groups you need for throwing, catching, and staying balanced when an opponent crashes into your space.

1
Butterfly Stretch

How to Do It:

  • Sit on the floor with feet together and knees bent outward.
  • Hold your feet with your hands and gently push your knees toward the floor.
  • Keep your back straight and hold the stretch.
  • Optional: Pretend your legs are butterfly wings and gently flap them!

Benefits: Stretches the inner thighs and hips.

2
Forearm Plank

How to Do It:

  • Get into a plank position with arms straight and back flat.
  • Hold for 30 seconds without dropping your belly.
  • Challenge: Try tapping one shoulder at a time while holding the plank.

Modification: Try a knee plank if needed.

Benefits: Builds core and upper body strength.

3
Seated Forward Stretch

How to Do It:

  • Sit on the floor with legs straight in front of you.
  • Reach forward toward your toes while keeping your legs straight.
  • Hold the stretch for 10 seconds, then sit up slowly.

Benefits: Stretches hamstrings and lower back.

quizzes.title: Quiz 1: Why We Move + Warm-Ups & Cool-Downs

questions.text: Marcus has 10 minutes before kickoff. Choose the BEST way for him to spend that time as a sport scientist would advise.

answers.text: Sit on the bench so his muscles stay rested and fresh for the game.
5 minutes of light jogging followed by 5 minutes of dynamic stretches like leg swings and arm circles.
10 minutes of long static stretches (each held for 60 seconds) — flexibility is always good before a game.
Eat a large meal so he has fuel for the next 90 minutes.

questions.text: Why does a proper warm-up measurably IMPROVE performance — not just reduce injury risk?

answers.text: It tricks the brain into thinking exercise is already over so muscles relax.
It cools muscles so they save energy until they are needed.
It raises core body temperature, increases blood flow to muscles, and lubricates joints so muscles produce force faster.
It burns enough calories to give you extra fuel during the workout.

questions.text: Which body system has the primary job of delivering oxygen to working muscles?

answers.text: The skeletal system.
The cardiovascular system.
The nervous system.
The digestive system.

questions.text: Static stretches (holds) done before sprinting can actually reduce peak power by up to 5%, which is why sport scientists recommend dynamic stretching before activity and saving static holds for the cool-down.

answers.text: True
False

questions.text: What is the brain chemical released during exercise that improves mood and reduces the perception of pain? (Starts with E, plural form.)

answers.text: endorphins
endorphin

questions.text: Sara has been complaining that she gets injured almost every season of basketball — usually a pulled hamstring or a sore knee. She tells you she 'just doesn't bother warming up because it wastes time.' (1) Using what you know about how the warm-up affects the body, predict TWO specific things happening in Sara's muscles when she starts a game cold. quizzes.title: Quiz 2: Strength, Endurance & Cardio

questions.text: What is the DIFFERENCE between muscular strength and muscular endurance?

answers.text: Strength is for boys; endurance is for girls.
Strength is the maximum force a muscle can produce in one effort; endurance is how long a muscle can keep producing force.
Strength only uses arms; endurance only uses legs.
Strength is built with cardio; endurance is built with stretching.

questions.text: Jada sprints at maximum effort for 8 seconds during a 60-meter dash. Which energy system is dominant?

answers.text: Oxidative — steady aerobic use of oxygen.
ATP-PC — used for all-out efforts under 10 seconds.
Glycolytic — used for efforts of 30 seconds to 2 minutes.
Digestive — breaking down breakfast for fuel.

questions.text: Which of these is the BEST description of 'progressive overload'?

answers.text: Doing the exact same workout every week so your body memorizes it.
Gradually increasing training demand (reps, sets, or load) over time so the body keeps adapting.
Lifting the heaviest possible weight on the first day to shock the muscles.
Resting completely until you feel zero soreness.

questions.text: A 12-year-old's estimated maximum heart rate is about 208 beats per minute, calculated using the rough formula '220 minus your age.'

answers.text: True
False

questions.text: What four-letter framework do sport scientists use for organizing any training plan? The letters stand for Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type. (One word, all caps or lowercase.)

answers.text: FITT
fitt

(1) Using the principle of progressive overload, explain WHY his progress has stalled. quizzes.title: Quiz 3: Flexibility & Nutrition

questions.text: What is the difference between active and passive flexibility?

answers.text: Active uses only your own muscles; passive uses outside help (gravity, a partner, or your hands).
Active happens during games; passive happens while sleeping.
Active is for warm-ups; passive is only for athletes.
They are the same thing measured differently.

questions.text: Mia finishes a 60-minute intense soccer practice. To take advantage of the protein synthesis window for muscle recovery, which snack within the next 1–2 hours is BEST?

answers.text: A bag of plain potato chips (mostly salt and fat).
A glass of chocolate milk (carbs + protein) and a piece of fruit.
Nothing — eating after a workout slows recovery.
Just water — she only lost water, not nutrients.

questions.text: Riley wants to touch their toes by the end of the month. Which plan uses the principle of SPECIFICITY most effectively?

answers.text: Touch their toes once a week, very hard.
Hold a static toe-touch stretch for 20–30 seconds, 3–5 times a week, for 4 weeks.
Eat bananas every day — they're flexible by nature.
Bounce up and down quickly while reaching for their toes for 60 seconds.

questions.text: Your muscles use carbohydrates as their preferred fuel and store extra carbs in your muscles and liver as glycogen — which is why distance athletes 'carb load' before long events.

answers.text: True
False

questions.text: What minerals — like sodium, potassium, and magnesium — does the body lose through heavy sweating, and which conduct electrical signals in nerves and muscles? (One word, plural.)

answers.text: electrolytes
electrolyte

questions.text: During a hot outdoor practice a player first gets painful calf cramps, then later becomes dizzy, nauseous, and is sweating heavily. These come from fluid and electrolyte loss. In order from earliest warning to most dangerous, what are the three heat illnesses?

answers.text: Heat cramps → heat exhaustion → heat stroke.
Heat stroke → heat cramps → heat exhaustion.
Dehydration → sunburn → fever.
Heat exhaustion → heat cramps → heat rash.

questions.text: An ad claims a $40 'fat-burning' tea will 'melt belly fat in 7 days — studies show!' and shows one customer's before/after photo as proof. Using a sport scientist's fact-vs-fallacy tests, what is the BEST reason to be skeptical?

answers.text: The price is too low for it to possibly work.
It promises fast, spot-specific fat loss and offers a single testimonial instead of a real, repeatable study.
Tea can never have any effect on the body.
Only supplements sold as pills are ever worth buying.
